title: ODNI & CIA Hacks Show an Escalating AI Cyber Arms Race, and the Client Side Is Especially Vulnerable as the Holiday Shopping Season Begins
summary: AI is defending the server and infrastructure. Can it defend the client side the same way? Why websites and mobile apps need AI-driven defense heading into Black Friday and Cyber Monday.
body_markdown:
*AI Is Defending the Server and Infrastructure. Can It Defend the Client Side the Same Way?*


**The short version:** The New York Times reported Tuesday that hackers breached a CIA and ODNI network. Who did it and how they got in haven’t been disclosed. The breach lands days after the Director of National Intelligence warned that AI is helping attackers strike at a scale nobody has seen. Most of the industry’s AI defense has gone to servers, networks and identities, while attackers are increasingly turning AI on the client side, the websites and mobile apps where customers log in and pay. An AI-driven defense on the client side is now critical to stopping those attacks, and it has never mattered more than this week, as Americans travel for Thanksgiving and shop online through Black Friday and Cyber Monday.


## A breach at the top of the target list


[The New York Times reported](https://www.ctvnews.ca/sci-tech/article/us-cia-odni-suffer-cybersecurity-breach-of-some-unclassified-information-nyt-reports/) on Tuesday that hackers got inside a CIA and ODNI network. Officials haven’t said how the attackers got in or who they are, and nothing reported so far points to websites or third-party code. What the breach does show is the climate. Days earlier, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton warned that AI is letting attackers strike at a scale nobody has seen, which is why organizations everywhere are racing to patch at once. He also told Americans to expect more disruptions as systems are upgraded, just as the country heads into one of the busiest travel weeks of the year. For every security team, the takeaway is the pace of the AI cyber arms race: attackers have new tools, and defenses have to keep up.


## AI went to the server room first


Security teams have spent the year putting AI to work where security budgets have always gone: finding and patching server flaws, and detection and response for the network, the endpoint and the identity layer. That work matters, and this month’s record patch volumes show how hard teams are running. All of those tools have one thing in common, though. They watch systems the company owns.


The client side is different. A typical checkout page loads dozens of scripts from outside vendors, and mobile apps carry SDKs that teams rarely review after launch. That code runs on the customer’s device and changes whenever its vendor changes it. Server, network and identity tools don’t see it, and AI-driven defense on the client side is still far less common than on infrastructure. Security and compliance teams still answer for it, and PCI DSS 4.0.1 Requirements 6.4.3 and 11.6.1 make that explicit for payment pages.


This week raises the stakes. Millions of Americans are booking flights, checking in on airline and hotel apps, and doing their holiday shopping on phones and laptops from Black Friday through Cyber Monday. Every one of those checkout pages and apps loads third-party code, and the busiest shopping days of the year are when a compromised script reaches the most customers and is hardest to spot in the traffic.


## The client side is where attackers keep winning


The details of the CIA and ODNI breach may never be public, but this year’s other headline attacks are well documented, and many of them came through the client side. Attackers are increasingly aiming AI at websites and mobile apps. It helps them find the cheapest way in, and that keeps turning out to be trusted third-party code, because compromising one vendor puts their code on every site and app that loads it.


In November, the attack researchers named[OPTIMJACK](https://www.feroot.com/blog/optimizely-breach-third-party-supply-chain-attacks/) abused a flaw in a testing platform’s signup process and planted a card skimmer that at least 178 organizations served to visitors for about 16 hours, straight from the vendor’s own CDN.[Polymarket was hit twice](https://www.feroot.com/blog/lessons-from-the-polymarket-breach/) through trusted third-party code that drained users’ wallets, and[AppsFlyer's JavaScript SDK was compromised](https://www.feroot.com/blog/appsflyers-javascript-sdk-has-been-compromised/) to deliver malicious code to the sites that ran it. Even[PHP2Shell](https://www.feroot.com/blog/php2shell-cve-2026-109618-cve-2026-109619/) , a server flaw found with help from AI, matters most for what an attacker could leave running on the pages customers load. In every case, the organizations’ servers were not where the damage showed up.


## Bringing AI to the client side


Feroot works with security and compliance teams that are accountable for code they didn’t write and can’t easily see. Our AI-powered platform watches the digital experience layer, the code that actually runs in customers’ browsers and mobile apps, and judges every script by what it does, whoever wrote it. The plan has three steps:


1. **See everything.** Map every script on login, checkout and account pages, including what tag managers load, and with MobileGuard, the third-party code inside mobile apps.
2. **Catch the change.**[DXSecure](https://www.feroot.com/dxsecure/) uses AI to learn how each script normally behaves and raises an alert the moment one starts reading payment fields or sending data somewhere new.
3. **Stop it and prove it.**[PaymentGuard](https://www.feroot.com/pci-paymentguard/) controls what can run on payment pages and keeps the evidence auditors ask for under PCI DSS 4.0.1.


A skimmer that goes live on Black Friday can collect card data from every holiday shopper who reaches checkout before anyone notices. Teams without client-side visibility tend to learn about a compromised vendor from a card brand or a customer, weeks after the skimmer went live, and then spend a quarter explaining it to the board and the QSA. Teams with AI watching the client side see the change within minutes, block it before it reaches customers, and hand over the documentation. Server-side AI should keep doing its job. Attacks that move at machine speed on the client side can only be stopped by a defense that also uses AI, watching every script, all the time.
